name: Data quality
summary: Data is accurate, complete, valid, and fresh — enforced by contracts, tests, and observability rather than assumed.
description: Data quality is the degree to which data is accurate, complete, valid, timely, and fit for use. High-quality architectures enforce expectations at the boundary with contracts and validation tests, refine raw inputs through curated layers, and watch for anomalies with observability instead of trusting inputs blindly. Low-quality designs land data as-is with schema-on-read and no enforcement, pushing every correctness burden onto downstream consumers.

mechanisms.name: Data contracts
mechanisms.note: Producer-consumer contracts pin schema, types, and semantics at the boundary so breaking or malformed data is rejected before it spreads.

mechanisms.name: Validation tests
mechanisms.note: Declarative expectation and assertion suites catch nulls, range violations, and referential breaks on every run before data is published.

mechanisms.name: Anomaly detection and observability
mechanisms.note: Continuous freshness, volume, and distribution monitoring surfaces silent regressions that pass explicit tests but still signal bad data.

mechanisms.name: Curated refinement layers
mechanisms.note: Progressively cleansing raw inputs through silver/curated stages deduplicates, conforms, and validates so gold outputs are trustworthy.

mechanisms.name: Quarantine of bad records
mechanisms.note: Routing rows that fail validation to a dead-letter or quarantine zone keeps clean tables clean while preserving rejects for repair.

manifestations.statement: Progressive bronze-to-silver-to-gold refinement with tests at each hop makes curated quality the explicit design goal of the architecture.
dbt tests on staging and marts assert not-null, uniqueness, and referential rules on every build, so quality is codified and enforced in CI.
Structured integration with full lineage and load auditing lets teams trace and validate every source contribution to the integrated core.
Matching, survivorship, and stewardship rules exist specifically to raise completeness and accuracy into trustworthy golden records.
Conformed dimensions and pre-load cleansing enforce validity and consistency so business reporting rests on curated, tested facts.
Identity resolution, deduplication, and enrichment are core to producing complete, accurate unified profiles fit for activation.
Data products ship with contracts and embedded quality checks as first-class SLAs, so each domain owns and guarantees its output quality.
Warehouse-native tests catch many issues, but load-first-transform-later means raw quality problems can surface downstream before they are caught.
The mirror is only as accurate as the source, and merge logic plus schema drift require monitoring to keep the replica trustworthy.
Device data can be noisy, dropped, or out of order, so quality depends on validation and gap detection applied after high-volume ingestion.
Streaming validation and expectations are feasible, but continuous commits and late-arriving events make thorough per-record checks harder than in batch.
Retrieval quality hinges on chunking, dedup, and freshness of the corpus, which need deliberate curation that pipelines often under-invest in.
Inline stream checks catch some issues, but validating completeness across an unbounded stream is inherently harder than gating a finite batch.
Transform-before-load allows cleansing en route, but quality depends entirely on rules coded into brittle jobs with limited observability.
Schema-on-read landing with no enforcement means everything arrives as-is; quality is unmanaged and pushed entirely onto downstream consumers.
Raw high-volume events arrive with malformed, duplicate, and bot traffic, so trustworthy metrics require heavy downstream cleansing not present at ingest.
Reading sources in place means their varying, unvetted quality is inherited directly, with no shared layer to validate or cleanse before serving.
Legacy on-prem sources carry accumulated quality debt, and incremental sync propagates those defects into the cloud unless separately remediated.
Governed sharing contracts and agreed schemas give consumers a defined, validated surface, though quality still depends on the provider's upstream curation.
Classification and policy enforcement keep sensitive fields well-governed, but masking and tokenization can obscure values enough to complicate downstream quality checks.
Centralizing metric logic removes definitional drift and copy-paste errors, though it governs calculation correctness rather than the quality of the underlying rows.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Validation, quarantine, and reconciliation steps sit inline in the pipeline, delaying when records become available for downstream consumption.

tradeoffs.title: Throughput
tradeoffs.note: Running constraint, freshness, and integrity checks on every batch consumes compute and slows the rate at which data can be ingested and published.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Sustaining high data quality requires observability tooling, test suites, and extra compute for profiling and reconciliation, all of which add ongoing cost.
